record.paper_title: Open Problems in Efficient Semi-Supervised PAC Learning
record.original_question: Let C be a concept class, let χ be a compatibility notion for unlabeled data, and let D be a data distribution. For ε > 0, define C_{D,χ}(ε) = {h ∈ C : 1 − χ(h, D) ≤ ε}. Assuming the target hypothesis belongs to C and is fully compatible with D, unlabeled data can in principle shrink the search space from C to C_{D,χ}(ε), so that information-theoretically one would hope to learn using on the order of (1/ε)(log |C_{D,χ}(ε)| + log(1/δ)) labeled examples, or a quantity polynomial in this bound. The open question is whether, for interesting choices of C and χ, there exist computationally efficient semi-supervised learning algorithms that achieve labeled-sample complexity matching this bound up to polynomial factors.

evidence.quote: For a given class C, compatibility notion χ, and distribution D, define CD,χ(ε) = {h ∈ C : 1 − χ(h, D) ≤ ε}. Under the assumption that the target belongs to C and is fully compatible, then given enough unlabeled data we can in principle reduce our search space from C down to CD,χ(ε). Thus, we should in principle need at most O(1/ε (log |CD,χ(ε)| + log 1/δ)) labeled examples to learn well.
The high-level question is whether for interesting classes C and notions of compatibility χ, one can learn with this many (or polynomial in this many) labeled examples by efficient algorithms.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be an instance space and let $C \subseteq \{0,1\}^X$ be a concept class. A compatibility notion is a function $\chi : C \times \mathcal{P}(X) \to [0,1]$, where $\mathcal{P}(X)$ denotes a class of probability distributions on $X$; the quantity $\chi(h,D)$ measures how compatible a hypothesis $h \in C$ is with an unlabeled data distribution $D$ (for instance, $1-\chi(h,D)$ might equal the probability that $h$ cuts through a high-density region, or some other unlabeled-data-based regularizer).

For a distribution $D$ on $X$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, define the reduced class
$$C_{D,\chi}(\varepsilon) \;=\; \{\, h \in C : 1 - \chi(h, D) \le \varepsilon \,\}.$$
Assume the learning model is realizable and compatible: there is an unknown target concept $c^* \in C$ with $\chi(c^*, D) = 1$, and the learner receives i.i.d. labeled examples $(x, c^*(x))$ with $x \sim D$, together with an arbitrary amount of i.i.d. unlabeled examples drawn from $D$.

Information-theoretically, given sufficient unlabeled data one can restrict attention to $C_{D,\chi}(\varepsilon)$, so that
$$m(\varepsilon, \delta) \;=\; O\!\left( \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\bigl( \log |C_{D,\chi}(\varepsilon)| + \log(1/\delta) \bigr) \right)$$
labeled examples suffice (with an analogous VC-dimension bound for infinite classes) to output, with probability at least $1-\delta$, a hypothesis of error at most $\varepsilon$.

Question: For interesting choices of the concept class $C$ and the compatibility notion $\chi$, does there exist a computationally efficient learning algorithm (running in time polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$, $\log(1/\delta)$, and the natural representation size of $C$) whose labeled-sample complexity is polynomial in $m(\varepsilon, \delta)$ above, while using polynomially many unlabeled examples?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as a broad open direction in efficient semi-supervised PAC learning. No general resolution has been published; subsequent work has produced positive results for specific classes and compatibility notions (e.g., co-training, cluster-based, margin-based assumptions) but not a general efficient algorithm matching the unlabeled-data-reduced sample complexity for arbitrary interesting $(C,\chi)$.

status_evidence.title: A PAC-Style Model for Learning from Labeled and Unlabeled Data (Balcan & Blum)
status_evidence.snippet: Defines compatibility χ and the reduced class C_{D,χ}(ε), and raises whether efficient algorithms can match the labeled-sample bound O((1/ε)(log|C_{D,χ}(ε)| + log 1/δ)) for interesting C and χ.
status_evidence.claim: The question is framed as an open direction with only special-case positive results known.
